title: We can generate code in seconds. Are we building better software?
body: AI-assisted development is changing how we write, test and deliver software. Productivity is going up. But someone still has to ask about the quality, maintainability and security of the code being generated.

The question took me back to my research on CK metrics and software fault prediction. I asked whether coupling (CBO) still predicts faulty classes once class size is controlled. The evidence says the CK metrics do predict faulty classes, but only until size is taken into account. Measuring software quality is not as simple as reading one number or checking that the code works.

In the age of AI this matters even more. AI can generate code, but engineering judgement, validation and accountability cannot be prompted away. Perhaps it is time to measure not only how fast we build software, but how well we build it.
This portfolio tries to practise that. Every push is measured by the pipeline (tests, coverage, complexity and architecture rules), and the result is shown on the Home page.

title: What does a great tech lead need to be good at in the AI era?
body: For a while I watched AI change how my team writes software. Code that took a day started taking an hour. Reviews got faster. Juniors ramped up quicker.

So I kept asking one question: if AI writes more of the code, what does a great tech lead need to be good at? My answer is designing the systems, making the hard trade-offs, and leading people through the change.

I wanted to get ahead of that shift, not just keep up with it. After more than six years at Winjit Technologies, growing from intern to Project Engineer, I moved from India to Ireland and became a student again. I am now doing an MSc in Software Engineering (Architecture and Project Management) at the University of Limerick.
Some days I am the most experienced person in the room. Other days I am the one asking the basic questions. Both feel right.

title: Lehman's laws, seen from inside a loan origination platform
body: Lehman wrote his laws about large systems in the 1970s, and I still meet them every sprint. Our consumer vehicle loan origination platform at Winjit is a set of .NET microservices that handle applications, document checks and credit decisions.

Continuing change shows up first. Every new lender rule, scorecard or document type means the system has to change, or it becomes less useful to the people who rely on it. We never reach a finished state.

Increasing complexity is the law you can feel. Each rule we add makes the next one harder unless we spend time on refactoring. We now reserve part of each sprint for that work, and we treat it as planned work, not as a favour.
The lesson I am taking into the MSc: evolution is the normal state of real software. The design question is how to make change cheap, safe and visible.

title: Week one in Limerick: from writing code to studying how code changes
body: After more than six years at Winjit in Nashik, I have started the MSc in Software Engineering at the University of Limerick.

The Software Evolution module is the one I was most curious about. In industry we talk about legacy code, technical debt and refactoring every day, but we rarely use a shared vocabulary for them. This module gives me that vocabulary.

This portfolio is part of that work. Version 1 is the first release, and the Readme page records every change as a typed maintenance activity, so the site itself becomes an example of software evolution.

title: Adding a new bank to an OCR pipeline is an adaptive change
body: Our bank statement extractor reads PDF statements from several banks and turns them into structured transactions. Each bank lays its statement out differently, so each one needs its own positional extractor, with Google Gemini as a fallback when the layout is unclear.

When we added two more banks, no requirement changed for users. The environment changed: new input formats arrived. In the maintenance taxonomy (Lientz and Swanson, later ISO/IEC 14764) that is adaptive maintenance.

The bug fixes that followed were corrective: sign errors, misread digits, batches cut short and a race condition in parallel processing. Adding validation and de-duplication was preventive work, because it stops the next class of errors before users see them.
Labelling each change this way made our sprint reviews clearer. It also showed us that most of our effort was not new features at all.
